His grandfather had died on a Tuesday; it was now Saturday; in between, Anthony had gone to school on Wednesday and Thursday, had laughed at Marcus's impression of their chemistry teacher on Friday, had eaten three meals a day and slept, mostly, through the night. Somewhere he had picked up the idea that grief had stages, that you moved through them in order like checkpoints, and if you skipped one, if you laughed four days out, you were doing it wrong. The car behind them honked, gently, and his father went.

His backpack was on the floor by his feet. In it was the AP Psychology textbook he'd been reading before any of this happened, chapters assigned for the fall semester he was supposedly preparing for, and he pulled it out now because there was nothing else to do with his hands. He hadn't planned to look anything up. He turned to the index, found bereavement, then grief, then loss, and followed a page number to a section on mourning.

His mother watched him in the visor mirror. "Homework? Today?"

"It's not homework." He read the page twice. A psychologist named George Bonanno had followed bereaved people over time, the book said, and what he found was that resilience was common, more common than anyone had assumed, and that there were no mandatory stages that everyone must pass through after a loss. Anthony read the sentence again. No mandatory stages. He had been operating for four days on the belief that there was a correct way to do this and that he was failing at it, and here was a man with a clipboard, apparently, who had watched actual widows and actual grandchildren and found that most of them functioned, laughed, kept eating, and that this was not a defect in them.

"That face you're making," his father said. "What?"

"Nothing. This chapter." He almost put the book down. Then he didn't. "Did you cry?" he asked the back of his father's head. "I mean. When. You know."

His father changed lanes before he answered, which was a kind of answer itself. "At the hospital. And once at the diner, weirdly, when the waitress brought his usual coffee order without being asked." He cleared his throat. "Why, you haven't?"

"No. I mean a little at the viewing. Not since."

"There's no schedule, Anthony."

"I know that now. That's what I'm saying. I found it." He held up the book as though it were evidence, which it was. "This guy studied it. Resilience is actually common. People just keep going and it's normal. There's no set of stages everybody has to pass through." Saying it out loud changed something; the fact had been true on the page and became true in the car.

His mother was quiet for a long moment. "Your grandfather would have liked that you looked it up. He never trusted anything he couldn't check himself." She smiled at the window. "He spent an hour once with a mechanic arguing about the etiology of a rattling noise. Where it started, what caused it. He loved that word. Everything had an etiology with him."

The car turned onto the parkway, and the light through the trees strobed across his father's hands on the wheel, and Anthony watched it, half mesmerized, thinking that even Bonanno's finding had limits. It told him resilience was common; it didn't tell him whether his own resilience was real or just delayed, whether the crying was coming in a week or a month or whether it wasn't coming at all, and whether that would be worse. He could hold both ideas now. He was probably fine, and he did not entirely know yet. Both could be true. His grandfather, the most honest man he'd known, would have approved of stating it exactly that way, with the uncertainty left in.

"He paid for my first semester of books," Anthony said suddenly. "I never told you. He handed me an envelope in March and said don't make it altruistic in your mind, I'm not being generous, I'm investing, you'll owe me conversations when you're in college. That's what I could say. At the open part."

His mother turned around again, and his father's eyes found him in the mirror, briefly, before returning to the road.

"Say that," his father said. "Say exactly that."

They pulled into the funeral home lot at ten fifty-two, gravel popping under the tires, his uncle already standing on the steps in a tie the color of a plum. Anthony put the textbook back in the bag, straightened the jacket that smelled of cedar, and got out of the car.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: The United Kingdom's standard rate of VAT, a sales tax built into most prices, has been 20 percent since January 4, 2011.
story:
The paycheque came in a thin envelope with the week's schedule, and Noah read it standing in the passageway between the kitchen and the washrooms, where the smell of fryer oil was thickest. He had worked sixty-one hours over two weeks at fourteen dollars an hour, which he had already calculated on his phone three times, but the number on the line marked NET PAY was smaller by an amount that made his stomach tighten. Above it, in smaller print, sat a column of deductions: income tax, CPP, EI. He folded the envelope into his back pocket and went back to clearing table nine.

He was saving for a ticket to London. His brother Marcus had moved there in September, and their mother had said, in the flat voice she used for things she couldn't change, that if Noah wanted to see him before Christmas, he'd be paying his own way. The cheapest flight was six hundred and eighty dollars, and the envelope in his pocket brought his total to five hundred and eleven. Two more pay periods, if nothing went wrong. He stacked plates and did the arithmetic again, as though the deductions might have shrunk.

At table four, a woman with reading glasses was interrogating her bill. "Why is it a hundred and two dollars when the menu said eighty-nine?" she asked her husband, and Noah slowed his bussing to half speed, the way Priya had taught him, so he could listen without seeming to.

"Tax," the husband said. "It's not on the menu prices. Thirteen percent, added at the end."

"That's absurd. In London it's just in the price."

Noah's ears went hot. Marcus had sent him a photograph two nights ago, a receipt from a café near his flat, and Noah had spent twenty minutes on it with the calculator app, confused, because nothing on it looked like the bills at the restaurant. The total was simply the total. He had texted Marcus and gotten back only "VAT," which told him nothing.

Priya was folding napkins behind the host stand when he came around the corner. "The woman at four says in England the sales tax is already in the price."

"It's called VAT," Priya said, not looking up. "My cousin in Manchester goes on about it."

He looked it up on his phone in the dry storage room, between the sacks of rice. Value added tax, the standard rate in the United Kingdom, had been twenty percent since January 4, 2011. He sat on a crate and worked it backwards on the calculator: if the tax was inside the price, then a receipt for twelve pounds carried two pounds of tax already paid, quietly, invisibly, the way salt is already in the bread. At the restaurant, the tax arrived at the end like a verdict. Same money leaving, different theatre. He caught himself thinking it was a difference of semantics, then corrected himself, because it wasn't just the words; it was what you could see and what you couldn't, and he wasn't sure which he trusted less.

That night, closing, he counted his tips at the far end of the bar while Priya ran the till. Cash tips were endemic to the place, the owner pretended not to know about them, and Noah had been adding them to his flight fund in a jar at home, three and four dollars at a time. He had counted forty-eight dollars tonight. It wasn't enough, and he knew it wasn't enough, and he pushed the bills around on the bar as though rearranging them might breed.

"Your till's out," Priya said suddenly, in a low voice, from the register.

"How much?"

"Over. Twenty-two dollars and forty cents." She held the tape up, then lowered it. "That's the table four bill exactly. The woman paid cash and I never closed it."

Noah stood very still. Twenty-two forty, sitting in the drawer, money that wasn't hers and wasn't his, money that would close the gap between him and January by one more shift. Nobody would ever know; the woman was gone, the owner was gone, and Priya was looking at him the way people look at you when they've decided to let you decide.

He thought about the receipt with the tax buried inside it, everything already settled before you saw it, and he thought about his paycheque's neat columns, everything itemized and still somehow opaque. Two ways of arranging the same unavoidable losses. He had liked to believe the visible one was the honest one. He wasn't sure he believed it anymore, and he was honest enough with himself to leave that question open.

"Run it as a payment on account," he said. "We'll tell Marco in the morning and refund it if she comes back." Priya nodded once and turned to the till, and Noah swept the last of the napkins off the bar into the bin.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex, published in 1949, contains the line usually translated as 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman', arguing that society shapes womanhood.
story:
Jaxon found his mother at the kitchen table with three novels fanned out in front of her and a legal pad covered in her slanted handwriting. "Book club's at seven," she said without looking up. "And I'm supposed to lead it, and I still don't know what I think." The clock above the stove read 4:40.

He set his backpack down slowly. His AP Literature teacher had spent the last two weeks on critical lenses, and tomorrow morning, first period, Jaxon had to turn in an essay applying a feminist lens to a passage from Jane Eyre. He had a photocopied page in his bag, flagged with a pink sticky note, and he had nothing written yet.

"Which book?" he asked, pulling out a chair.

"Pride and Prejudice. We're arguing whether Elizabeth Bennet's choices are really hers." She rubbed her eyes. "Deb thinks Lizzy marrying Darcy is true love and self-determination. Priya says it's just the best deal available to a woman with no money and no sons. It's my job to keep it from becoming a shouting match."

Jaxon spread his photocopy on the table beside her legal pad. The passage was the one where Jane agrees to marry Rochester, all tremor and submission. "We could trade problems," he said. "You help me with my essay, I help you with your debate."

His mother laughed, a short tired sound, but she slid her chair around to his side of the table. He could smell the orange peel she'd left on a saucer, and the radiator ticking under the window carried the smell of dust going warm.

"Okay," he said, reading aloud. "So the feminist lens. My teacher says you ask who has power in the scene, and who's doing the looking, and who's being looked at." He paused. "Rochester keeps saying he'll dress Jane in jewels and silks. She keeps saying no. That part's easy. What's hard is that Jane wants the marriage too. So is her wanting hers, or is it the wanting she was trained to have?"

His mother pulled the legal pad closer and started writing. "That's exactly Priya's argument about Lizzy."

"Wait." He got up and went to the bookshelf in the hallway, the low one by the coat rack, where his mother kept the books from her college years, their spines gone soft. He ran a finger along them and pulled out a thick one, its cover a faded gray. He'd seen it once when he was ten and thought it looked boring. Inside the front cover his mother had written her maiden name and a date. He carried it back to the kitchen.

"The Second Sex," his mother read off the spine. "Simone de Beauvoir. That's from 1949." She flipped through it, pages whispering. "There's a line in here. 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.' I underlined it. Look, it goes through everything, society, childhood, all of it, that's her whole argument, that society shapes womanhood."

Jaxon copied the line onto his legal pad, pressing hard. "So if that's true, then Jane's wanting isn't fake, exactly. It's real wanting, but it's built wanting. She lives in a world where marrying Rochester is the biggest thing a woman can do, so of course the biggest feeling she has points at him."

"Then Lizzy's love isn't a lie either," his mother said slowly. "It's just that she fell in love inside a very small room."

"Priya's going to malign Darcy's proposal no matter what," Jaxon said. "And Deb will act like money is a peccadillo compared to passion. You could say they're both right about half of it."

His mother looked at him. "Say that again."

"Say what again?"

"The small room. Say it the way you just said it." She wrote it down, word for word, and he watched her do it, and something in his chest went loose and warm.

The clock said 5:25. He still had four paragraphs to draft and she had to make the pasta salad she'd promised Priya. She stood, filled the big pot, set it on the burner, and while the water heated she read his opening paragraph out loud, stumbling once over "patriarchal gaze," and he crossed it out and wrote "who does the looking" above it instead.

"One thing I can't figure out," he said, watching the water shiver toward a boil. "De Beauvoir says society makes the woman. But Jane still says no to the jewels. If she's fully trained, where does the no come from?"

His mother grated cheese into a bowl, knuckles working. "That's a good question for your essay. You don't have to answer it. You just have to be honest that it's open." Steam climbed the window and blurred the streetlight coming on outside.

At 6:40 she left, cake carrier in one hand, legal pad in the other, calling back through the door, "Text me if your conclusion is any good." Jaxon sat alone with the pot cooling and the gray book open on the table. He read the underlined line twice more, then wrote his final paragraph and left the last sentence hanging on a question. He took a photo of it and sent it to his mother, then closed the book and set it back on the low shelf, spine out, where he could find it again.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: Mirrors leave blind spots beside and behind a car, so a quick look over the shoulder is needed before merging or changing lanes.
story:
The cones were set up behind the grocery store, in the far corner of the lot where the cart returns never quite reached, and Madison's father had promised that if she could park between them three times in a row, he would take her on the highway that same afternoon. She had backed in twice already, each time crooked but inside the lines, and now she sat with her hands at ten and two, breathing on the windshield, studying the gap in the mirror.

"Third one," her father said from the passenger seat, eating sunflower seeds he'd bought inside. "You've got more room than you think."

"That's what people say to make you feel better about having less room than you think."

He laughed, shells clicking against his teeth. She reversed slowly, turned the wheel hand over hand, and came to rest close enough to the rear cone that she could have touched it through the open window. Not perfect, but legal. She left the engine running and looked at him until he shrugged.

"Fine. Three in a row. Highway it is."

The on-ramp near the store was short and steep, the kind that gave you about eight seconds to get up to speed, and Madison had been dreading it for two weeks. Her instructor at school, a pugnacious retired cop named Mr. Vasquez who seemed to take personal offense at hesitation, had told her class that merging was where people failed, not because they couldn't drive but because they trusted their mirrors. She'd written it in her notebook without really understanding it.

Now she accelerated down the ramp, watching the side mirror, which showed a lane of empty gray asphalt, and she began to drift left. Her shoulder turned for a half second, a reflex she hadn't planned, and there was a sedan beside her, silver, close enough that she could see the driver's coffee mug on the roof of her own mouth-shaped reflection in its window. She pulled back level in her lane, heart going like a dropped metronome.

"There was a car there the whole time," she said.

"Yep." Her father cracked another seed. "Mirrors leave blind spots beside and behind you. That's why you look over your shoulder, every time. Vasquez didn't cover that?"

"He covered it. I just didn't believe him."

"It's not a matter of belief," her father said, in the mild tone he used when he was enjoying being right. "It's geometry. Or physics. One of the sciences."

She merged properly at the next opening, chin over her shoulder, signal on, and it was almost anticlimactic, how easy it was once she actually looked. The highway unrolled ahead, bland and sunlit, big-box stores giving way to pines. She held her speed and let the wheel settle.

What interested her, driving home in the right lane, was that both things were true. The mirrors were useful; they showed her most of what was behind her, and she would not give them up. And they were incomplete in a way that mattered exactly when it mattered most, in the seconds before a decision. Mr. Vasquez had wanted her to distrust the mirrors entirely, as if they were out to deceive her, and her father wanted her to trust the shoulder check with the same blind faith she'd wrongly given the glass. She thought neither position was quite right, though she couldn't yet say what the right one was, except that it involved looking twice and believing once.

Back at the grocery store, her father went in for more sunflower seeds and she stayed in the car, rearranging the mirrors, small adjustments, tilt and angle, until the view in the glass overlapped better with the view over her shoulder. It didn't fix everything. There would still be a wedge she couldn't see, and she accepted that now instead of resenting it.

Her phone buzzed. A text from Priya, who had failed her test twice: how was the highway. Madison typed back that it was fine, then deleted it, then typed the truth: almost merged into a silver car, mirror looked empty, shoulder check saved me. Do the shoulder check. Priya.

When her father came out with the seeds and a receipt he'd been examining like a document that might impugn him, a gallon of milk charged twice, she started the engine. He pointed at the cones still standing in the far corner of the lot.

"One more," he said. "For complicity's sake. I was the one who said you had more room than you think."

"You were right, though."

"I know. That's the worst part."

She backed in on the first try, straighter than the others, and sat there a moment with the engine idling, looking from the mirror to the window and back again, seeing two slightly different pictures of the same quiet lot.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: Home equity is the home's current value minus what is still owed on the mortgage.
story:
Juliette took the last seat in the bank's waiting area, between a man talking too loudly into his phone and a woman rocking a stroller with her foot, and pulled the folder of papers her grandmother had thrust at her that morning into her lap. The folder smelled of lavender and pencil shavings. Inside were the deed to a small brick house on Felton Street, a statement from a savings account opened in 1968, and a sticky note in her grandmother's slanted hand: Ask about the equity. And don't let them charm you.

She was third in line. The man beside her was arguing with someone about a deposit that hadn't cleared, and the word "deposit" kept landing like a small hammer. Juliette had learned the word at fourteen, when she'd handed a cashier a jar of birthday money for her first checking account and watched the teller type it into a machine as though it were nothing. Money going in. That was all a deposit meant, though she'd felt, at the time, that something larger should happen, some ceremony.

"Number forty-one," the speaker announced, and the stroller went up. Then forty-two, the loud man. Juliette smoothed the folder on her knee and thought about the argument from last night, which was really the argument from every night that week. Her grandmother wanted to sell the Felton Street house and give Juliette the proceeds toward a down payment on an apartment, since Juliette was starting at the university in September and the campus rentals were devouring her part-time wages. Her mother said it was too much, that Grandmere had earned that house, that Juliette should take the student loans like everyone else and stop letting an old woman rearrange her whole life around a girl who hadn't even picked a major.

Grandmere's neighbor, Mrs. Okafor, had sold her own house on the same street in the spring, and Juliette had been at the kitchen table when Grandmere heard what Mrs. Okafor walked away with. It was less than anyone expected. "She still owed on it," Grandmere said, tapping the table with two fingers. "The bank took its share first." She'd looked at Juliette then with an expression that demanded understanding, and Juliette, not wanting to admit she had none, had nodded and gone home and looked it up at midnight in the blue light of her laptop: home equity is the home's current value minus what is still owed on the mortgage. She'd read it three times. Then she'd found a forum where a man in Ohio complained that he'd owned his house for nine years and still had almost no equity, and a woman replied that ownership was a ladder you climbed slowly, and Juliette had closed the laptop feeling both informed and vaguely cheated, as though the ladder had been advertised as an escalator.

"Number forty-three." She stood too fast and her chair scraped. The teller was younger than expected, maybe twenty-five, with a name tag that said DARA and a pen she was already spinning.

"I need to know what my grandmother's house would actually give her," Juliette said, laying out the deed. "She owns it outright. No mortgage. And I need to know what a down payment on an apartment would look like, because she wants to give me the money and my mother thinks it's chicanery, her word, of the emotional kind."

Dara stopped spinning the pen. "Emotional chicanery. That's a good phrase." She pulled the deed closer. "Okay, so if there's no mortgage, then the equity is the whole current value. Every dollar of the sale price, minus fees, is hers. Your neighbor, if she still owed money, she'd only keep the value of the house minus what was still owed on the mortgage. That's the difference. Your grandmother keeps more because she owes nothing."

Juliette wrote this down even though she knew it, because writing it down made it true in a way that knowing it at midnight hadn't. Dara, warming to the subject the way people do when someone under twenty actually asks, explained that a down payment was usually some fraction of the price, that the mortgage covered the rest, and that rent, by contrast, was money that never came back to you at all. "You're paying for the right to exist in the space," Dara said. "Which is not nothing. I rent. I exist in a very nice space above a laundromat." She grinned. "It smells like dryer sheets and I've learned to love it."

The dryer sheets line startled a laugh out of Juliette, loud enough that the stroller woman looked over and almost smiled herself. "The thing is," Juliette said, quieter, "I don't know if I should take it. She sold her wedding rings two years ago to cover the property tax. My mother says taking the house money makes me the kind of person who lets people sell their houses for her."

"Or it makes you the kind of person who owns something at nineteen instead of paying rent into a hole until you're forty." Dara slid a pamphlet across the counter, then pulled it back. "Actually, don't take the pamphlet. Pamphlets are where hope goes to die. Talk to a mortgage officer, that desk over there, and talk to your mother tonight, not on the phone, at the table." She stamped something on a slip of paper and handed it over. "That's a referral, not a decision."

Outside, the afternoon had the hot metallic smell of July pavement. Juliette sat on the bank's wide stone steps and called her grandmother, watching a pigeon commandeer a sandwich crust from a smaller pigeon with total impunity. "Well?" Grandmere said before hello. "What did they say?"

"That you'd keep almost everything," Juliette said. "Because you don't owe anything on it. The whole value is yours."

There was a silence on the line, long enough that Juliette could hear the kitchen radio, the one that only got the classical station. "Then come to dinner," her grandmother said finally, "and bring your mother, and bring that face you make when you've decided something and won't say it." Juliette looked at the slip of paper in her hand, at the referral, not a decision, and at the pigeon now eating like a king on the steps below her. "I haven't decided," she said. "I'm working on it."

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Montana is the one US state where, after a probationary period, an employer generally needs good cause to fire a worker, under its 1987 Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act.
story:
Madeline had circled the help wanted sign in the window of Hartwell's Hardware twice on her walk past, once in the morning and once after her interview, as though the circling itself might hold the position open. The manager, a wide, deliberate woman named Ruth, had asked her three questions, none of them about hardware, and then said she would call by Friday. That left four days for Madeline to want the job with an intensity that embarrassed her a little, since the work was stocking shelves and mixing paint on Saturdays.

She told her cousin Dara about it that night over video, because Dara, nineteen and already working at a warehouse in Ohio, had opinions about everything and a phone plan that made the calls free. "So did your boss seem normal?" Dara asked, chewing something off camera, a gourmand even from a bag of gas station trail mix, narrating each handful.

"She seemed fine. Quiet."

"Quiet's fine until it isn't. My old supervisor got quiet and then fired Jayden on a Tuesday because he was in a bad mood. That's it. That was the whole reason." Dara leaned closer to the lens. "Bosses can just do that here. Fire you for nothing."

Madeline said she didn't think that was true everywhere, and Dara said name one place, and neither of them could, so the argument dissolved the way theirs always did, into a bet of ten dollars and a promise to look it up, which Madeline suspected Dara would forget by morning.

She didn't forget. She sat on her bed with her laptop and found it in twenty minutes, scrolling past forums full of people who were certain and wrong. Her mother had been from Billings, and the summer Madeline was nine she'd spent three weeks there while her parents sorted things out, a month of dry grass and her uncle's loud kitchen. She remembered her uncle saying, once, over burgers, that out there a job was a job, they couldn't just toss you off it, and she'd assumed at nine that this was a feeling, not a law. It was a law. Montana, the one state in the country where, after a probationary period, an employer generally needed good cause to fire someone. There was even a name for it, the Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act, from 1987, printed in plain type at the top of the page. Everywhere else, the sites agreed with Dara in the flat tone of settled fact. She texted her cousin the link and the ten dollars became a question of honor.

On Friday, Ruth called while Madeline was slicing a mango badly at the counter, and offered her the Saturdays, and then paused in a way that made Madeline grip the knife handle. "One thing. It wouldn't be just stocking. Saturdays we run the paint counter, and I lost my mixer in April, so you'd be on your own by June. It's a lot of standing there with nothing happening, and then a rush. Some people find the dead air desensitizes them to customers, honestly, they stop seeing the person and just see the can. I need someone who doesn't do that."

Madeline said she didn't think she would. She was thinking of her mother, actually, who had waited tables for years and could still, at forty, ask a stranger what they needed in a voice that made the question real. She wanted to be like that, though she understood even as she thought it that wanting a quality and having it were separated by years of Saturdays she hadn't worked yet.

Ruth was noncommittal, in the way of a person who had heard promises before, and said to come Monday at eight. When Madeline hung up, she texted Dara the news, and Dara replied with a wall of congratulations and then, forty minutes later, a separate message: "okay so my friend tomas just got let go from the warehouse. for nothing. I checked. we're in ohio." Madeline read it twice, sitting on the floor with mango juice drying on her fingers, and felt the fact settle somewhere between triumph and uselessness, a rule that protected exactly one state's worth of cousins, hers included, since her mother had come from the one place it counted.

On Monday she arrived at seven forty. Ruth was already at the paint counter, teaching herself something from a laminated sheet, and she looked up when the bell rang and pointed at the aprons on the hook with her chin. Madeline took the smallest one, still too big, and tied it while Ruth slid a can of eggshell white across the counter toward her and said, "Mix me this. And tell me why you're standing like you're about to apologize."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Chemist Michel Eugène Chevreul published his law of simultaneous contrast in 1839, describing how a color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it.
story:
The craft cabin smelled of pine sap and turpentine, and by Wednesday afternoon Kaitlyn had painted the same gray sky four times. The assignment for Friday night's exhibition was simple enough: a landscape of the lake and the ridge behind it, any medium, done by suppertime or it didn't hang. Her problem was stranger than the deadline. On the left side of the canvas, where the gray met the orange of a sun-baked rock face, the sky looked warm, almost dusty rose. On the right, above the blue water, the identical gray, mixed from the same jar in one sitting, looked cold and faintly blue-green. She had not touched the paint between them. She leaned close until her nose almost grazed the canvas, then stepped back to the doorway, and the sky kept splitting into two skies.

"Your gray's dirty," said Rosa from the next easel, without looking up from her clay owl. "You probably didn't clean your brush."

"I cleaned it." Kaitlyn held the brush up like evidence in a trial. "Same water, same rag, same everything. It's the same gray."

"Then your eyes are dirty." Rosa smiled to show she was joking, mostly. Kaitlyn let it go, because arguing would impugn nothing except Rosa's certainty, and Rosa's certainty was not the sort of thing that yielded. Still, she covered the right half of the sky with a scrap of paperboard and stared at the left. Warm. She moved the paperboard. Cool. She did this five times, quickly, like a magician proving there was no trick, and each time the gray changed its mind.

The camp's bookshelf, four sagging planks of mildewed paperbacks behind the ping-pong table, was nobody's idea of a library. But the art counselor, who was off driving the van to town until five, kept a few of her own books there, and Kaitlyn went looking with her hands still tacky with paint. She found a fat volume with a cracked spine, half biography and half color plates, about a French chemist named Michel Eugène Chevreul. She read standing up, one hip against the shelf, while two boys argued over whether the top of the ping-pong table was legally a desk. Chevreul, she read, had published his law of simultaneous contrast in 1839, and the law said that a color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it. She read the sentence twice. She looked at her own hands, then at the window, then at the page again.

From the doorway of the rec hall, Deb Chen watched the girl with the paint-stained fingers stand absolutely still over a book for what had to be ten minutes. Deb had come in for the ping-pong paddles and had stayed because stillness like that was rare at the camp, rarer than loons. She could see the open page from where she stood: a diagram of small squares nested inside larger squares, gray inside orange, gray inside blue. The girl, Kaitlyn, Deb remembered, from the awkward first-night name games, touched one small square with one finger, very carefully, the way you'd touch a moth. Then she closed the book, tucked it under her arm without asking, and walked out fast, heading for the craft cabin, and Deb picked up the paddles and thought no more about it, except that she hoped somebody would hang that book back up eventually.

In the cabin, Kaitlyn dragged her canvas into the light by the window. The complement of orange was blue; the complement of blue was orange. So her gray, sitting beside orange rock, drifted toward blue, which should have made it cooler, not warmer. She frowned at that. Maybe she had the complements backwards, or maybe the shifting worked in some way the sentence didn't say, because the sentence only said toward the complement of the neighboring color, and her gray was neighbor to orange on one side and blue on the other, and it looked warm on the orange side. She did not know which part she was getting wrong. What she knew was that the gray was not one thing, and that the painting could use that, if she had the nerve to let it.

Rosa came over at six, carrying her finished owl, which had a metamorphic look, as though it might at any moment become a different and better owl. She stood in front of the canvas while Kaitlyn worked a thin line of violet into the rocks.

"It's called simultaneous contrast," Kaitlyn said, not stopping. "Chevreul, 1839. The gray shifts toward the complement of whatever's next to it. That's why it's two colors."

"That's the same gray?"

"Same gray."

Rosa was quiet for a moment. "You're not going to fix it, then."

"I don't think it's broken." Kaitlyn stepped back and looked at the sky, warm over the rocks, cool over the water, one gray doing the work of two. Whether the painting was honest or whether it was an accident she had decided to call a plan, she could not entirely say, and there was no time to decide before Friday. The show started at seven. She picked up the paperboard scrap, held it over the left sky one more time, and watched the warmth go out of the gray like a tide pulling back from shore.

"Hand me the violet," she said, and Rosa did.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: In C major the dominant seventh chord is G7, made of the notes G, B, D and F, and it pulls strongly toward the C major chord.
story:
The practice rooms at Halloway Concert Hall were in the basement, below the stage, and you could hear the floorboards flex when the orchestra rehearsed above. Logan had claimed room four every Tuesday since September because it had the piano with the least dead keys. He spread his staff paper on the music stand and set his pencil down crosswise, the way his older sister had shown him years ago, though she had stopped playing before she finished high school.

The assignment was sixteen bars, a melody with chord changes, written in standard notation by Friday. His teacher, Mr. Okafor, had said only that endings matter more than beginnings, because a listener forgives a weak first phrase but remembers a weak last one. Logan had written fifteen bars that he almost liked. The melody rose through the first eight, settled in the middle, and by bar fifteen it had walked itself home to a C major chord. It should have felt finished. It felt like a door closing on a room with nothing in it.

He played the fifteen bars through, then the last chord, then sat with his hands in his lap. In the key of C, he had been using C, F, and G chords, the ones every beginner used, and the melody sat on top of them the way a cat sits on a warm car, comfortable and going nowhere. Above him the orchestra had stopped. A tuba player laughed at something in the hallway.

Theo knocked and came in without waiting. Theo was a second-year composition student who wore the same green coat in every season and who agreed, in Logan's experience, with whatever the last person in the room had said. Logan had privately labeled him a sycophant and felt some guilt about it, since Theo's flattery was at least sincere, unlike the kind that wants something.

"Sixteen bars," Logan said. "Mine ends on C and it sounds like the melody just got tired."

"Maybe tired is honest," Theo said, and then, when Logan said nothing, "or maybe it's not. Could be both." Everything Theo said was equivocal, but he played piano better than Logan did, so Logan slid over on the bench.

"Play bars fourteen and fifteen." Theo played them. The melody's last phrase ended on an E, held over a C major chord, and then silence. Theo played it again and this time, without being asked, added a G chord under the second-to-last melody note and put an F on top of it with his right hand. Suddenly the final C chord did not just arrive. It received something.

Logan pulled the staff paper toward him. "What did you add? Tell me the notes."

Theo spread his right hand so Logan could see. "G, B, D, and F. It's a dominant seventh, on G." He said it as if naming a sandwich he'd ordered a hundred times, then added, "People put it before the end all the time. You'll hear it in practically anything upstairs." He stood, checked his phone, and left with a compliment about Logan's bar nine that Logan did not believe and accepted anyway.

Logan wrote the four notes into bar fifteen, stacked in the notation he had learned that month, stem directions checked twice. He played the ending with the new chord, and the sound of the G, B, D and F pulled his ear forward into the C major chord the way a held breath pulls toward release. He did not fully understand it. He had been told his whole life that music theory was a set of rules, and this felt less like a rule than a fact about gravity he had stepped off a curb and noticed. He wrote the chord symbol above the staff and drew a bracket from it to bar sixteen.

At the Thursday rehearsal, Logan sat in the last row of the concert hall with the paper on his knee. The student orchestra was running a slow piece that ended with four repetitions of a final phrase, and on the third one the strings dropped low and the horns took a chord that he recognized by shape, that same tilted, leaning sound. The whole audience, he could feel it, leaned with it. Whatever the chord was doing, it did not need to be understood to work, and Logan found this both reassuring and slightly annoying, because it meant his earlier endings had failed in a way he hadn't been able to hear until tonight.

In room four on Friday morning he made a choice. He kept the dominant seventh in bar fifteen, but he also kept a version on a second sheet without it, labeled with the date, filed in the folder under his sister's old exercise books. When Mr. Okafor collected the sixteen bars that afternoon, he played Logan's ending once, said "Better," and moved to the next student's paper. Logan sat in the basement afterward with the folder open on the piano lid, both endings side by side, and played them alternately until he could no longer decide which one he preferred, and then played the version with the added note one more time.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In 1868 the Senate acquitted President Andrew Johnson by one vote: 35 senators voted to convict, one short of the two-thirds needed.
story:
The gymnasium smelled of floor wax and folding chairs, and Lucas arrived early enough to claim a seat near the microphone that stood at the center aisle. He had come with a page of notes he'd copied out the night before, though he'd told his mother he was going for the free pizza the student council had promised. The town hall meeting had been called to debate a resolution asking the state legislature to adopt a recall provision for local officials, and Lucas, who had spent three weeks arguing about impeachment in his government class, intended to speak. He wanted, more precisely, to be right in public, which felt different from being right in a classroom where only Mr. Okafor was listening.

The council members sat behind a long table draped in gray felt, and beside them, as a guest, sat a woman introduced only as Ms. Reyes, visiting from Ottawa. Lucas noticed her because she took notes in a small green book while everyone else typed on phones. When the mayor opened the floor, an old man in a barn coat was first to the microphone, saying that if the council could not remove a bad road commissioner, then the whole structure was a farce. People clapped in the scattered, uncertain way of crowds who agree with a sentiment but not yet with its consequences.

When Lucas's turn came, his palms were damp against his notes. He said that removing a leader should be hard, that the founders of presidential systems had made it deliberately difficult. "In 1868 the Senate acquitted President Andrew Johnson by one vote," he said. "Thirty-six senators voted to convict, one short of the two-thirds needed. So even when a president is hated, the bar stays high." He let that sit, pleased with the weight of it, and then added, "If we make removal too easy, every loser of an election will try to overturn it."

Ms. Reyes raised her hand, and the mayor, seeming relieved to have something to do, called on her. She stood without leaving her chair, holding the green book. "A parliamentary system works the other way," she said. "The head of government stays only as long as the legislature supports him. If his own party turns, a simple vote removes him. It is designed to be easy." She said it lightly, as if offering weather, and sat down. Lucas felt his argument tilt beneath him, because he had never actually thought about why two systems would choose opposite assumptions, only about which one was correct.

The old man in the barn coat came back to the microphone. "Young man," he said, and Lucas braced for dismissal, "you said thirty-six. It was thirty-five. I teach this, retired now, but I have transcribed that roll call more times than I care to admit. Thirty-five voted to convict. One vote short." He paused. "Edmund Ross was the one everyone remembers, but the number is thirty-five." Lucas looked down at his notes and saw his own handwriting, the six written in a fast, sloppy loop, and could not remember whether he had miscounted or miscopied. The veracity of everything else on the page suddenly seemed provisional. "Either way," he said, and heard how weak it sounded, "one vote decided it."

"That's exactly the point," Ms. Reyes said from her seat, and several people laughed, not unkindly. "One vote, in both directions." Lucas stood there with the microphone still live and the whole gymnasium waiting, and instead of defending his six, he found himself thinking about what the two systems disagreed on. A parliamentary system trusts the legislature to judge constantly, in real time, without ceremony. A presidential system trusts the fixed term more than it trusts any majority, and so it raises the bar until removal becomes almost metamorphic, something that almost never happens, and when it does, it changes everything. He could not decide which mistrust was wiser. He suspected the answer depended on what you were afraid of.

"I got the number wrong," Lucas said into the microphone. The old man nodded once, like a judge accepting a plea. "But the number being close is the interesting part. Maybe the bar is too high. Maybe a prime minister can be removed too easily, by a bad week. But it can't be both." He looked at Ms. Reyes, who was writing in her green book again, and he wondered what she thought of a town arguing about a road commissioner as if it were the fate of a nation. Someone called out that they were debating a county drainage board, not the presidency, and the room laughed properly this time.

The mayor moved the resolution to a vote of the council, and Lucas sat down and watched the hands. The clerk read the tally slowly, as though she too understood the weight of margins. Five in favor. Six against. It failed by one vote, and the old man in the barn coat stood up, put on his hat, and said loudly enough for the first three rows to hear, "Well. History repeats." Lucas stayed in his seat while the chairs were stacked, copying the corrected number onto a fresh page in his own notebook, pressing hard enough that the five came through onto the next sheet.

On his way out, Ms. Reyes was waiting by the door with her coat over her arm. "You changed your mind up there," she said. "Most people don't." Lucas shrugged, still unsure whether that was a compliment or a diagnosis. "I changed one number," he said. "The mind part's still out for deliberation." She smiled and held the door open for him, and the cold outside hit his face like a splash of water.
